claim: Wolsing et al. (ANRW 2019) found that in lossy networks QUIC clearly outperforms the stock TCP+TLS+HTTP/2 web stack, which the authors mainly attribute to QUIC progressing streams independently of head-of-line blocking.
quote: In lossy networks, QUIC clearly outperforms the current Web stack, which we mainly attribute to its ability to progress streams independently of head-of-line blocking.

claim: Wolsing et al. found that QUIC still outperforms a tuned variant of TCP, although the gap narrows once TCP is tuned.
quote: Nevertheless, QUIC still outperforms even our tuned variant of TCP.

claim: Wolsing et al. report that tuning TCP parameters (initial window, pacing, BBR, kernel buffers) is not negligible and yields significant gains, so untuned TCP baselines overstate QUIC's advantage.
quote: In this paper, we can show that tuning TCP parameters is not negligible and directly yields significant improvements.

claim: Wolsing et al. attribute QUIC's performance advantage mostly to its reduced RTT during connection establishment, with head-of-line-blocking avoidance mattering mainly on lossy networks.
quote: This performance advantage is mostly caused by QUIC's reduced RTT design during connection establishment,

claim: Yu and Benson (WWW 2021), measuring production QUIC at Google, Facebook and Cloudflare, found that removing head-of-line blocking has little impact on Page Load Time and Speed Index relative to congestion control for real-world web pages. This is evidence against HOL blocking being the main lossy-network benefit.
quote: QUIC's removal of HOL blocking has little impact on Page Load Time and Speed Index relative to congestion control for real-world web-pages.

claim: Yu and Benson found that QUIC's overall performance is largely determined by the server's choice of congestion-control algorithm and the robustness of its implementation under edge-case network conditions, which can matter more than the protocol design.
quote: its overall performance is largely determined by the server's choice of congestion-control algorithm

claim: Yu and Benson conclude that QUIC's performance is tied to implementation design choices, bugs and configuration, so QUIC measurements often do not generalize across deployments.
quote: QUIC's performance is inherently tied to implementation design choices, bugs, and configurations

claim: An early (2016) KTH thesis using Chromium's QUIC toy client and traffic shaping found that packet loss affected TCP and QUIC throughput similarly, a result against a clear QUIC advantage under loss. The study predates the IETF QUIC standard and is small in scope.
quote: Results were similar for the two transport protocols.

claim: Liu et al. (arXiv 2409.16267, 2024) compare HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 with proxies under emulated loss and report that HTTP/3 performs best under high loss and high latency, leveraging connection migration and multiplexing.
quote: H3 excels under high-loss and high-latency conditions, leveraging connection migration and multiplexing

claim: Arxiv 2309.16395 measured QUIC implementations on real hardware and found that QUIC throughput varies widely across client and server implementations, so a single QUIC-vs-TCP result does not generalize. This is a caveat rather than a loss measurement.
quote: Our results show that QUIC performance varies widely between client and server implementations from 90 Mbit/s to 4900 Mbit/s.

claim: In a multi-stream test (20 x 1 MB files), HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 performed comparably when packet loss was below 8%; at 8% or more loss HTTP/3 significantly outperformed HTTP/2.
quote: when the packet loss reaches or exceeds 8%, H3 significantly outperforms H2.

claim: At 12% packet loss with no proxy, HTTP/2 averaged 113.42 s to complete the multi-stream download while HTTP/3 finished in 20.98 s.
quote: at 12% packet loss without a proxy, H2 required an average of 113.42 seconds to complete the download

claim: During a simulated IP address change (connection migration) under 4% loss and 50 ms delay, the HTTP/2 client averaged 56.7 s versus 6.6 s for HTTP/3 (no proxy).
quote: under conditions of 4% packet loss and 50ms delay, the H2 client (wget_h2_resume) took an average of 56.7 seconds

claim: QUIC connection migration lets an ongoing session survive an IP change, which the paper contrasts with TCP needing a new connection after an IP change.
quote: QUIC's connection migration allows an ongoing session to continue without interruption

claim: The paper caveats that HTTP/2 with the right congestion control algorithm can achieve performance comparable to HTTP/3, so the protocol gap depends on CCA choice.
quote: H2 with the right congestion control algorithm (CCA) can achieve performance comparable to H3.

claim: In a Lighthouse-based HTTP/3 (draft 27) vs TCP+TLSv1.3 study with NetEm loss capped at 1.4%, HTTP/3 scored better at higher loss rates and its score flattened as loss rose while TCP's decayed almost linearly.
quote: H3's aggregate score flattened out as more loss was introduced whereas TCP+TLSv1.3's curve decayed almost linearly.

claim: The same study found results became unstable beyond 1.4% packet loss in NetEm, and those trials were excluded.
quote: Beyond the setting of 1.4% packet loss in NetEm, the results became quite unstable.

claim: In the same study, TCP+TLSv1.3 still scored higher than HTTP/3 at 2000 ms delay, while the gap narrowed approaching 1000 ms delay.
quote: TCP+TLSv1.3 still performed better in a trial with 2000ms delay.

claim: Measured on a Pixel 5 phone over 5G testbeds, QUIC (HTTP/3) performed worse than HTTP/2 for 1 GB downloads and the paper says the gap is larger on weaker mobile clients.
quote: On weaker clients such as mobile devices, the gap is even larger.

claim: The paper reports QUIC performs worse than HTTP/2 in Ethernet and 5G scenarios, attributing it to high bandwidth saturating client CPU rather than to packet loss.
quote: QUIC performs worse than HTTP/2 in Ethernet and 5G scenarios.

claim: The paper states QUIC's video bitrate degradation is hidden over 4G but appears over 5G, because QoE degradation only shows when underlying bandwidth is high.
quote: For example, the impact is hidden over 4G but unleashed over 5G.

claim: For 4G, the authors report the QUIC vs HTTP/2 performance difference is not that significant, with HTTP/2 slightly better overall bitrate.
quote: the performance difference is not that significant

claim: Over real operational MONROE mobile networks in Europe, QUIC-based operations were advantageous for users that move, and performance was strongly affected by the chosen QUIC congestion control algorithm (no loss rates reported in the abstract).
quote: QUIC-based operations are advantageous for users that move, and they are also strongly affected by the congestion control algorithm chosen for QUIC.

claim: The MONROE study states QUIC reacts better than TCP to the variations of channel quality experienced by mobile nodes.
quote: QUIC reacts better to the vagaries of channel quality experienced by mobile nodes.

claim: On fast networks, the UDP+QUIC+HTTP/3 stack suffers a data rate reduction of up to 45.2% versus TCP+TLS+HTTP/2 in file download tests (Zhang et al., WWW 2024).
quote: the UDP+QUIC+HTTP/3 stack suffers a data rate reduction of up to 45.2% compared to the TCP+TLS+HTTP/2 counterpart

claim: The authors identify the root cause of QUIC's slowdown on fast networks as high receiver-side processing overhead, including excessive data packets and QUIC's user-space ACKs.
quote: we identify the root cause to be high receiver-side processing overhead, in particular, excessive data packets and QUIC's user-space ACKs

claim: At higher bandwidth, QUIC consistently lags behind HTTP/2 in throughput by up to 15.7%, while the two perform similarly at lower bandwidth (below about 600 Mbps).
quote: QUIC consistently lags behind HTTP/2 by up to 15.7% in terms of throughput

claim: QUIC and HTTP/2 perform similarly only when bandwidth is relatively low (below about 600 Mbps), so the QUIC penalty is a high-bandwidth effect rather than a lossy-link effect in this study.
quote: QUIC and HTTP/2 exhibit similar performance when the network bandwidth is relatively low (below ~600 Mbps)

claim: During packet reception, QUIC incurs considerably higher CPU usage than HTTP/2 on state-of-the-art client hosts.
quote: during packet reception, QUIC incurs considerably higher CPU usage than HTTP/2 on state-of-the-art client hosts

claim: The QUIC throughput gap also reduces application quality: video streaming shows up to a 9.8% video bitrate reduction.
quote: video streaming (up to 9.8% video bitrate reduction)

claim: In a YouTube measurement over 2600 hours, the TCP setup either outperformed or matched QUIC-enabled playback in more than 60% of cases.
quote: the legacy setup (TCP) either outperforms or performs the same as the QUIC-enabled browser for more than 60% of cases

claim: QUIC's fallback to TCP is blind: it does not distinguish middlebox-caused failures from congestion-caused failures, which can hurt performance.
quote: not distinguishing between failures caused by middleboxes and that caused by network congestion

claim: Measurement studies cited by the IETF put the share of networks that block all UDP traffic at roughly 3% to 5%, so UDP blocking affects a minority of networks.
quote: Measurement studies have shown between 3% [Trammell16] and 5% [Swett16] of networks block all UDP traffic

claim: Falling back from QUIC to TCP loses stream multiplexing, which would then have to be implemented in the application layer.
quote: TCP does not provide stream multiplexing, and therefore stream multiplexing would need to be implemented

claim: The IETF applicability document reports little evidence of systematic disadvantage to UDP traffic compared to TCP, which cuts against the assumption that UDP is generally throttled.
quote: there is little evidence of other forms of systematic disadvantage to UDP traffic compared to TCP

claim: QUIC in NGINX (2019 era) sent one UDP packet per sendmsg() call, adding per-packet syscall and context-switch overhead that Cloudflare later reduced with GSO.
quote: Currently the code that implements QUIC in NGINX uses the sendmsg() system call to send a single UDP packet at a time.

claim: In a Cloudflare 2020 test on their own network, HTTP/3 was slightly slower than HTTP/2 on a larger page (2.33s vs 2.30s), which the authors suspect stems from a congestion-control mismatch (BBR on HTTP/2 vs CUBIC on HTTP/3).
quote: HTTP/3 is just slightly slower than HTTP/2 on our network today, taking 2.33s to load versus 2.30s.

claim: On mobile devices, QUIC's advantage over TCP diminishes across the board and is at times not statistically significant, although QUIC outperforms TCP in most mobile cases.
quote: Its advantages, however, diminish across the board and at times are not statistically significant.

claim: In competition with TCP, QUIC can take more than its fair share of bottleneck bandwidth (always more than half in the reported experiments) because it achieves a larger congestion window.
quote: our experiments showed that QUIC always consumes more than half of the bottleneck bandwidth

claim: Meta (Facebook app video, QUIC vs TCP): mean time between rebuffering improved in aggregate by up to 22%, depending on platform.
quote: Mean time between rebuffering (MTBR), a measure of the time between buffering events, improved in aggregate by up to 22 percent, depending on the platform.

claim: Meta (Facebook app video, QUIC vs TCP): the rate of video stalls was reduced by 20%.
quote: The rate of video stalls was reduced by 20 percent.

claim: Meta reports QUIC's video benefit was outsized on networks with poorer conditions, especially in emerging markets.
quote: QUIC improved the video viewing experience, with an outsized impact on networks with relatively poorer conditions, especially those in emerging markets.

claim: Meta (Facebook app dynamic GraphQL requests, HTTP/3 vs HTTP/2): 6% fewer request errors and a 20% tail latency reduction.
quote: People on Facebook experienced a 6 percent reduction in request errors, a 20 percent tail latency reduction

claim: Uber (rider and driver apps, QUIC vs TCP over HTTPS): 10-30% reduction in tail-end latency at scale.
quote: We witnessed a reduction of 10-30 percent in tail-end latencies for HTTPS traffic at scale in our rider and driver apps.

claim: Uber's TCP traces found most connections were lossy, with TCP retransmitting 3.5% of total packets.
quote: most connections were lossy, causing TCP to retransmit 3.5 percent of total packets.

claim: Uber observed up to 7% of packets dropped by the network at congested sites.
quote: we witnessed as high as 7 percent of packets being dropped by the network.

claim: Uber: the 75th percentile of TCP back-off was almost three seconds, far above typical RTT on its networks.
quote: the 75th percentile of TCP back-off was almost three seconds.

claim: Google QUIC (as reported in Google's SIGCOMM 2017 paper, cited secondhand): search load time reduced 8% average on desktop and 3.6% on mobile.
quote: reported an 8% average reduction in the time it took to load Google search results on desktop and 3.6% on mobile.

claim: Google QUIC: for the slowest 1% of Google users, page load was up to 16% faster (as cited via Internet Society Pulse).
quote: And for the slowest 1% of Google users, it was up to 16% faster to load.

claim: Google QUIC: YouTube showed up to 20% less video stalling in economies such as India (as cited via Internet Society Pulse).
quote: up to 20% less video stalling

claim: Cloudflare 2020 real-browser tests on its own sites: HTTP/3 performance still trails HTTP/2 by about 1-4% on average in North America, which it attributed possibly to BBR vs CUBIC congestion control.
quote: HTTP/3 performance still trails HTTP/2 performance, by about 1-4% on average in North America.

claim: Cloudflare 2024 Speed Week (real user measurements, connection time, not page load): at P95, connection time is 116 ms faster with HTTP/3 enabled.
quote: At P95, Cloudflare is 116 ms faster for connection times when HTTP/3 is enabled.

claim: Akamai live stream in Latin America (April 2023): about 69% of HTTP/3 connections reached 5 Mbps or more, versus 56% of HTTP/2 connections.
quote: about 69% of HTTP/3 connections reach a throughput of 5 Mbps or more,

claim: Wix (connection setup, HTTP/3 vs HTTP/2): up to 33% improvement in the mean, and often more at the 75th percentile.
quote: up to 33% improvements in the mean and often more in the 75th percentile

claim: APNIC notes most public HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3 comparisons are lab-based rather than real-world deployments.
quote: most (public) comparisons between HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 are based on lab testing instead of real-world deployments.

claim: HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one TCP connection, but TCP loss recovery cannot see that parallelism, so one lost or reordered packet stalls all active transactions.
quote: However, because the parallel nature of HTTP/2's multiplexing is not visible to TCP's loss recovery mechanisms,

claim: A lost or reordered packet in HTTP/2 over TCP causes all active transactions to experience a stall.
quote: a lost or reordered packet causes all active transactions to experience a stall

claim: QUIC incorporates stream multiplexing and per-stream flow control at the transport layer, which HTTP/3 relies on.
quote: The QUIC transport protocol incorporates stream multiplexing and per-stream flow control,

claim: HTTP/3 provides reliability at the stream level while QUIC keeps congestion control across the whole connection.
quote: By providing reliability at the stream level and congestion control across the entire connection,

claim: In HTTP/3, stream concurrency is managed by QUIC rather than by the HTTP layer as in HTTP/2.
quote: In contrast to HTTP/2, stream concurrency in HTTP/3 is managed by QUIC.

claim: QUIC gives no ordering guarantee between bytes on different streams, so data ordering on one stream is independent of other streams.
quote: QUIC does not provide any means of ensuring ordering between bytes on different streams.

claim: QUIC streams can be created by either endpoint, send data concurrently interleaved with other streams, and be canceled.
quote: Streams can be created by either endpoint, can concurrently send data interleaved with other streams, and can be canceled.

claim: QUIC loss detection is tracked separately per packet number space, unlike RTT measurement and congestion control.
quote: Loss detection is separate per packet number space, unlike RTT measurement and congestion control

claim: QUIC packet numbers increase strictly within a packet number space and directly encode transmission order, which removes the retransmission ambiguity TCP has.
quote: QUIC's packet number is strictly increasing within a packet number space and directly encodes transmission order.

claim: TCP conflates transmission order at the sender with delivery order at the receiver, which RFC 9002 cites as the source of retransmission ambiguity.
quote: TCP conflates transmission order at the sender with delivery order at the receiver

claim: QUIC supports many ACK ranges, whereas TCP's SACK option provides only three.
quote: QUIC supports many ACK ranges, as opposed to TCP's three SACK ranges.

claim: RFC 9002 recommends a packet reordering threshold (kPacketThreshold) of 3 for declaring packets lost.
quote: The RECOMMENDED initial value for the packet reordering threshold (kPacketThreshold) is 3

claim: A PTO timer expiration does not by itself indicate packet loss; the sender must send an ack-eliciting probe packet instead.
quote: A PTO timer expiration event does not indicate packet loss

claim: RFC 9001 states that new QUIC connections can usually be established and secured within a single round trip only when there is no packet loss.
quote: Absent packet loss, most new connections can be established and secured within a single round trip;

claim: QUIC 0-RTT lets a client send application data before the handshake completes, by reusing parameters from a previous connection.
quote: The 0-RTT feature in QUIC allows a client to send application data before the handshake is complete.

claim: Using 0-RTT with HTTP/3 creates exposure to replay attacks.
quote: The use of 0-RTT with HTTP/3 creates an exposure to replay attack.

claim: QUIC connection migration uses connection identifiers to allow a connection to transfer to a new network path.
quote: Connection migration uses connection identifiers to allow connections to transfer to a new network path.

claim: In this QUIC version only clients can migrate connections.
quote: Only clients are able to migrate in this version of QUIC.

claim: After a migration, packets sent on the old path must not contribute to congestion control or RTT estimation for the new path.
quote: Packets sent on the old path MUST NOT contribute to congestion control or RTT estimation for the new path.

claim: RFC 9000 requires endpoints to perform path validation on a detected address change, unless the address was already validated.
quote: An endpoint MUST perform path validation
